overview: The Regency of Algiers developed within the Ottoman world around a Mediterranean port. Its history includes maritime diplomacy, artisans’ work and the everyday institutions of a densely built city. Surviving houses, fountains, textiles and agreements reveal different aspects of that society.

periods.title: An Ottoman port and fortified city
periods.summary: Algiers came under Ottoman protection in the early sixteenth century. Its administration changed over time, while the city developed within fortifications overlooking the Mediterranean.

periods.title: Deys, patrons and urban building
periods.summary: Deys headed the regency. Patrons supported public fountains through endowed property, and the waterfront neighborhood developed palaces alongside smaller homes and covered passages.

periods.title: Commerce regulated by treaty
periods.summary: The 1795 agreement with the United States specified duties, shipping protections and rules affecting captives. Its provisions reveal how commerce and coercion were entangled.

periods.title: New terms of maritime diplomacy
periods.summary: The 1815 agreement rejected tribute from the United States and required exchanges of captives. Such bilateral terms did not amount to universal freedom for enslaved people.

periods.title: The city after the regency
periods.summary: French capture ended the dey’s government in 1830. The city continued to be inhabited, and its surviving buildings underwent alterations, reuse and later conservation.

items.text: The Kasbah brought houses, markets, bathhouses, mosques and palaces together on a steep site. Builders worked with earthen bricks, lime and earth renders, stone and wood. This urban fabric connected worship, trade and household life; the architecture was an accumulation of building traditions rather than the work of one ruler.

Public fountains depended on both benefactors and administration. Donations of property, known as habus, supported their operation, while an official called the khudjat al-uyun oversaw the associated funds. Water supply therefore involved maintaining an institution as well as constructing a basin and channel.

An inscription dates a fountain commissioned by Husayn to 1820 near Bab al-Djazira. Its praise of the patron preserves his public message, not proof that everyone received enough water. Later records trace the fountain’s relocation, including a move in 1867, showing why a monument’s present setting may differ from its original one.

The Palais des Raïs preserves part of the waterfront neighborhood of Qaâ Es-Sour: palaces, sailors’ homes, a mosque, covered passages and a defensive battery. The site’s history dates Palace 18 to 1750 and records its purchase by Dey Mustapha Pacha in 1798. Elite residences belonged to a larger working urban district.

sections.title: Embroidery and the evidence of objects

items.text: An eighteenth-century turban cover in the Walters collection is embroidered in silk on linen. The museum explains that such cloths protected turbans when they were removed and stored without being unwound. An ornate textile could therefore serve a practical household purpose as well as expressing care for an item of dress.

The Walters record identifies an Algerian origin but gives no named maker or original wearer. Henry Walters’s acquisition date and method are unknown; the museum received the piece through his 1931 bequest. These gaps matter: a surviving object can document skilled work without revealing exactly who commissioned, used or transported it.

A separate eighteenth-century panel at the Metropolitan Museum combines linen, silk and metal-wrapped thread. Its catalog describes Algerian embroidery as receptive to designs from Istanbul while retaining distinctive colors and stitches. Exchange within the Ottoman world supported adaptation, rather than making every region’s textile work identical.

The 1795 treaty set a five-percent duty on American goods sold in the regency’s ports and permitted unsold goods to leave without that charge. This specific arrangement placed American merchants alongside several European trading partners. It describes negotiated rules, not unrestricted commerce for every visitor.

The same agreement protected some Americans against enslavement while still recognizing owners’ claims over captives. Article 11 required the return of fugitives reaching American warships; article 12 addressed negotiated redemption. These provisions show the limits of bilateral protection within an economy that continued to exploit enslaved people.

The edition warns that the original English version differed substantially from the Turkish text. J. H. Kramers therefore prepared a new translation in 1930. Comparing versions is part of historical research: apparent agreement between governments does not guarantee that surviving translations express identical obligations.

The 1815 treaty changed those terms. It rejected American tribute, required the release and exchange of captives, and allowed Christian captives reaching American warships to remain there. It also prohibited enslaving future prisoners captured between the two parties. These were defined protections, not a declaration abolishing slavery everywhere in the regency.

The dey signed a surrender agreement on 5 July 1830 after French forces landed in June. Resistance elsewhere continued, including under Ahmed Bey in the east and Abd el-Kader in central and western Algeria. The capture of the capital did not mean that the whole country immediately accepted French control.

Palais des Raïs later housed families before its evacuation for restoration. Work involved Algerian specialists and an Italian firm under UNESCO supervision, with work on site beginning in 1988. Its preserved appearance reflects conservation decisions as well as historical construction; the buildings also have a history of residential reuse.

ending.text: The regency ended with the French capture of Algiers in 1830. Its inhabitants and urban traditions continued. The imported map extends this record to 1878, which should not be read as the duration of the dey’s government.
